Family Outage Plan

Search the plan

First 10 minutes

If the lights and Wi-Fi go out, do these in order. Print this page and tape it inside a kitchen cabinet; a plan on a dead phone is no plan.

  1. Check your unit's breaker panel and look outside. If only your apartment is dark, it may be a tripped breaker or a building issue (call the leasing office's emergency line); if the block is dark, it's an outage.
  2. Report it to Austin Energy: call 512-322-9100, or text OUT to 287846.
  3. Turn on the battery radio: KLBJ 590 AM / 99.7 FM is the City of Austin's designated emergency-alert station.
  4. Put phones in low-power mode. Charge from a power bank, not the car, unless the car is outside with the garage door open.
  5. Unplug TVs, computers and other electronics to avoid a surge when power returns. Leave one lamp switched on so you know when it's back.
  6. Keep the fridge and freezer closed. Note the time the power went out.
  7. Fill the bathtub and a few pots with tap water right away; upper floors lose water pressure first. In Feb 2021 the city lost water after power failed at its largest treatment plant.
  8. Gather everyone in one room. Get flashlights out; no candles near kids.

Phased action plan

Most outages are short, but Feb 2021 ran for days, so plan as if this one will too. Each phase adds to the one before it.

Phase 1: Hour 0 to 24 (stay home, conserve)

  • ☐ Confirm the outage on the radio; listen at the top of each hour for scope and expected restore time.
  • ☐ Set phones to low power. Pick ONE phone to stay on for news; others off except at set check-in times (for example 9 am, 1 pm, 6 pm).
  • ☐ Text, don't call. Texts get through when networks are jammed. Send one group text to family with your status.
  • ☐ Eat from the fridge first, then freezer, then shelf-stable food.
  • ☐ Cold weather: move everyone to one interior room, close doors to unused rooms, hang blankets over windows.
  • ☐ Hot weather: the second floor heats up first. Close blinds on sunny sides, open windows only at night.
  • ☐ Check on the neighbors on each side, especially anyone elderly or with babies.

Phase 2: Days 1 to 3 (manage food, water, temperature)

  • ☐ Fridge food has passed its 4-hour safe window; keep only what stayed at 4°C or below. A full freezer holds about 48 hours closed.
  • ☐ Ration drinking water at 1 gallon per person per day; use tub water for flushing and washing.
  • ☐ Watch for a boil-water notice on the radio. If one is issued, boil or treat all tap water (Water section).
  • ☐ Charge devices from power banks or solar; recharge banks from the car only with the car outdoors.
  • ☐ Keep a simple log on paper: indoor temperature morning and night, water left, food left.
  • ☐ Decide each evening: is the house still safe for the kids tonight? (Evacuation section has the thresholds.)

Phase 3: Days 4 to 14 (sustain or relocate)

  • ☐ If roads are open, go to a library or rec center serving as a warming/cooling and charging center during its hours (Hampton Library at Oak Hill is 0.5 mi away).
  • ☐ Restock at H-E-B when it reopens; stores on generators often open with cash-only or limited hours. Bring cash.
  • ☐ Sanitation: if toilets can't flush, use the bucket-and-bag method (Water section).
  • ☐ Rotate sleep so one adult is awake on cold nights to watch the kids and any heat source.
  • ☐ Pool resources with neighbors: one person's camp stove, another's generator, shared watch.
  • ☐ Plan relocation to family or a hotel outside the outage zone if indoor temperatures or water become unsafe.

Phase 4: Beyond 2 weeks (long-term grid down)

  • ☐ Relocate if at all possible. A home without power, water and heat is not a safe place for a 2- and 4-year-old for weeks.
  • ☐ If you must stay, join or organize a neighborhood group: shared cooking, water collection, a rota for checking on vulnerable neighbors.
  • ☐ Register needs with 311 and 211; city shelters and supply points are announced on KLBJ 590 AM.
  • ☐ Keep medical needs ahead of time: refill prescriptions the moment any pharmacy opens.
  • ☐ Stay with your group; don't travel alone at night when streetlights and signals are out.

Heat, cold and cooking in an all-electric home

With no gas, your home loses all heat, cooling and cooking at once. The biggest danger is not the cold itself but unsafe heaters and stoves brought indoors: carbon monoxide kills families every Texas freeze.

Never indoors, not even in the garage

  • Generators, charcoal or propane grills, camp stoves meant for outdoors, car engines, patio heaters.
  • The oven or stovetop for heat (it won't work anyway without power, and a gas one at a neighbor's is just as dangerous).
  • Generators: most apartment leases ban them, and one running on a balcony or breezeway can push exhaust into your unit or a neighbor's. Use a portable power station instead.
  • Put a battery carbon monoxide alarm in the sleeping room. Buy one this week if you don't have one.

Staying warm (freeze, like Feb 2021)

  1. Pick the room with the fewest exterior walls and windows, usually a bedroom or the area by an interior hallway. Everyone sleeps there. A second-floor unit gains some warmth from the unit below, so close up early to hold it.
  2. Close doors to every other room. Roll towels against door gaps.
  3. Cover windows with blankets, quilts or cardboard; close blinds and curtains.
  4. Build a "tent" inside the room: a table or bunk covered with blankets, kids and adults inside together. Body heat in a small space adds up.
  5. Dress in layers: thermal base, fleece, coat, hat (most heat leaves from the head), wool socks. Change out of damp clothes immediately.
  6. Sleep on insulation, not the bare floor: sleeping pads, couch cushions, folded blankets under you.
  7. Eat and drink warm when you can. Calories produce heat; dehydration speeds hypothermia.
  8. Heat sources that are indoor-safe: a portable power station running a small electric blanket, hand warmers, hot water bottles filled from a pot heated outdoors.
  9. Protect pipes: open cabinet doors under sinks, let one faucet drip if the city hasn't asked you to conserve. Know where your main water shutoff is in case a pipe bursts.

Staying cool (summer outage, often over 38°C)

  1. Heat rises to the second floor. Close blinds and curtains on sunny windows by 9 am, and in the hottest hours take the kids down to a shaded spot, a cooling center or the car with A/C.
  2. Open windows only at night when it's cooler outside than inside; close them again in the morning.
  3. Wet cloths on the neck, wrists and feet; battery fans moving air across damp skin.
  4. Drink water on a schedule, not just when thirsty. Toddlers dehydrate fastest.
  5. In the hottest hours, go to a public cooling center (libraries and rec centers during open hours), or sit in a running car in an open driveway with A/C on.
  6. Never leave a child in a parked car, even for a minute.

Cooking without power

Method Where Notes
No-cook food Anywhere Canned meats and beans, peanut butter, crackers, cereal, fruit cups. Simplest and safest.
Butane camp stove Outdoors or in a well-ventilated area, per its label Store fuel canisters outside living areas.
Propane camp stove or grill At ground level only, 10+ ft from the building. Fire code generally bars open-flame grills on apartment balconies; use the complex's grill area if it has one Most reliable for boiling water. Keep 2 spare cylinders.
Charcoal grill Outdoors only Never bring smoldering coals inside to "warm the room."
Portable power station + kettle or hot plate Indoors Drains a battery fast: boil small amounts only.
Water and food

Store 1 gallon per person per day for 14 days; for your family of four that's 56 gallons. In an apartment, stackable 5-gallon containers under beds and in closets, plus a bathtub water bladder (about 100 gallons, filled at the start of an outage), make that fit. Austin's tap water depends on power at the treatment plants: in Feb 2021 a power loss at the Ullrich plant triggered a citywide boil-water notice that lasted about a week.

Water sources, in order of use

  1. Stored bottled water and filled containers (drinking, kids' cups, cooking).
  2. Bathtub and pots filled at the start of the outage (flushing, washing).
  3. Water heater tank, if your unit has its own (usually in a closet; ask the office if unsure), typically 40 to 50 gallons. Turn off its breaker first, let it cool, then drain from the valve at the bottom. Turn the breaker back on only after the tank is refilled.
  4. Ice in the freezer as it melts.
  5. Never: pool, creek or rainwater for drinking unless boiled or filtered and treated.

Making water safe

  • During a boil-water notice, Austin Water says to bring water to a rolling boil for 2 minutes, then cool before use.
  • No way to boil: use unscented household bleach. Per gallon of clear water, 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach. Stir, wait 30 minutes; it should smell faintly of chlorine. Double it for cloudy water, and filter cloudy water through a cloth first.
  • Kids' cups: use bottled water or water you've boiled. Shelf-stable milk boxes need no water or refrigeration; keep a supply.

Food safety

Item Safe window, door closed Rule
Refrigerator About 4 hours Throw out milk, meat, leftovers, cut fruit that sat above 4°C for 2+ hours
Full freezer About 48 hours Food with ice crystals or at 4°C or below can be refrozen
Half-full freezer About 24 hours Pack items together; add bags of ice
Breast milk (fridge) Use within the fridge's 4-hour window Move to a cooler with ice right away

When in doubt, throw it out. Keep a fridge thermometer inside so you're not guessing. In a winter outage you can store food in a cooler outdoors in shade, if it stays below 4°C and away from animals.

3-day no-cook menu for 4 (2 adults, ages 2 and 4)

Use this as the shopping list for the first 3 days; repeat or rotate it for 14. Buy foods the kids already eat, and pack a manual can opener.

Day Breakfast Lunch Dinner Kids' snacks
1 Dry cereal with shelf-stable milk boxes, bananas Peanut butter on crackers, applesauce pouches Canned chicken with crackers, canned corn, fruit cups Cheese sticks from the fridge (eat first), raisins
2 Granola bars, shelf-stable milk, canned peaches Tuna or chicken salad kits, pretzels, baby carrots (if still cold) Canned beans and rice cups (eaten room-temperature), canned green beans Fruit pouches, animal crackers
3 Instant oatmeal with hot water from the camp stove, or cereal Peanut butter and jelly on shelf-stable tortillas Canned ravioli or chili (heated at ground level if possible), applesauce Crackers, dried fruit

For the 2-year-old, cut anything round or firm into small pieces and skip whole nuts and popcorn.

Sanitation without water

  • Toilets still flush if you pour a bucket of water (about 1 to 2 gallons) straight into the bowl.
  • No water at all: line the toilet or a 5-gallon bucket with two heavy trash bags, add a scoop of kitty litter or sawdust after each use, tie off and store outside.
  • Hand sanitizer before eating and after diapers or the toilet. Stomach illness spreads fast when washing is limited.
Power, phones and communication

When internet and cell service fail, the radio is your news and pre-agreed meeting points are your phone. Settle the plan below with everyone in the house before you need it.

Keeping devices alive

  • Power banks: at least one 20,000 mAh bank per adult, kept charged. Each refills a phone roughly 3 to 4 times.
  • A portable power station (500 Wh or more) can run a CPAP, a small fan, an electric blanket or a router for hours. Pair it with a folding solar panel for multi-day outages.
  • Car charging: only with the car parked outside, never in a closed or open garage. Run the engine 30 minutes at a time and keep the tank at least half full from October through March.
  • Skip a gas generator: it isn't practical or usually allowed in an apartment. A power station (1,000 Wh or more) plus a folding solar panel on the balcony is the apartment alternative.
  • Turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, drop screen brightness, close apps. Airplane mode except at check-in times.

Getting information with no internet

  • Battery or hand-crank AM/FM/NOAA radio: KLBJ 590 AM / 99.7 FM for city alerts; NOAA WXK27 on 162.400 MHz for weather.
  • Phone emergency alerts (WEA) reach you over the cell network even when data is down. Keep them switched on.
  • Before the next outage, register at WarnCentralTexas.org for text, call and email alerts tied to your home address.
  • Text OUT to 287846 to report the outage and REG to the same number to get Austin Energy status texts.

Also write down: the leasing office and after-hours maintenance numbers, your building and unit number, any gate code, and the two nearest stairways out of your building.

Write these numbers on paper in every adult's wallet and every child's backpack. Young kids should know their full name, a parent's name and phone number, and the meeting point.

Our apartment is the family meeting point: if anyone gets separated during an outage, everyone heads home. The spot outside the building covers fires and anything else that keeps you out, so pick it and show it to the kids.

Medical guide

The nearest 24-hour ER is St. David's Emergency Center at Circle C, about 1 mile from the park; for a seriously ill or injured child, Dell Children's in Mueller is the region's pediatric hospital, about 11 miles away. This guide is first aid until help arrives, not a substitute for it. A CPR and first-aid class (Red Cross or AHA) is the single best prep step on this page.

Call 911 or go to the ER now

  • Not breathing, blue lips, choking that back blows and chest thrusts don't clear
  • Unconscious, confused, seizing, or can't be woken
  • Suspected carbon monoxide poisoning (get everyone outside first)
  • Bleeding that soaks through a pressure dressing
  • A child with fever who is very hard to wake, has a stiff neck, trouble breathing, or a rash that doesn't fade when pressed
  • Signs of heat stroke or severe hypothermia (below)

If 911 won't connect, text 911, or drive to Fire/EMS Station 27 on McCarty Ln (1.1 mi north); stations are staffed around the clock.

Emergencies an outage makes more likely

Condition Warning signs What to do
Carbon monoxide poisoning Headache, dizziness, nausea, sleepiness, several people or pets sick at once; better when away from home Everyone outside into fresh air immediately. Call 911 from outside. Don't go back in.
Hypothermia Shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness, confusion; toddlers: cold red skin, unusual fussiness or very low energy. Shivering that stops is worse, not better Move to the warmest spot, remove wet clothes, warm the chest and core first with blankets and skin-to-skin contact, warm sweet drinks if fully alert. Call 911 if confused or drowsy.
Frostbite Numb, white or grayish-yellow, waxy skin on fingers, toes, ears, nose Warm gently in warm (not hot) water. Don't rub it. Don't rewarm if it may refreeze. Get care.
Heat exhaustion Heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, weakness, nausea, headache, fast pulse Cool place, loosen clothes, wet cloths, sips of water. Get care if vomiting or not better within an hour.
Heat stroke Body temp 39.5°C or higher, hot red skin (dry or damp), confusion, fast strong pulse, passing out Call 911. Cool aggressively: cold water, ice packs at neck, armpits and groin. No fluids if not fully alert.
Dehydration (kids) No wet diaper or potty trip in 8 hours, no tears when crying, dry mouth, unusually sleepy Small frequent sips of oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte), a sip every few minutes. Get care if no improvement.
Burns Red, blistered or white/charred skin Cool running water 10 to 20 minutes (no ice, butter or ointment). Cover loosely with a clean dressing. Large burns, face, hands, or a child's burn: get care.
Deep cuts, heavy bleeding Blood pooling or spurting Firm direct pressure with gauze for 10 minutes without peeking. Add layers, don't remove. Tourniquet above the wound for limb bleeding you can't control.
Food poisoning Vomiting, diarrhea after eating questionable food Fluids, rest. Get care for blood in stool, high fever, or signs of dehydration.

Medications to keep on hand

Stock a 2-week supply of everything below for a family of 2 adults and children aged 2 and 4. Kids get children's formulas only: dose by your child's weight using the chart on that product's label and the measuring device in its box, never a cut-down adult dose. Ask your pediatrician for a printed dosing chart for both kids at the next visit and keep it with the kit.

For the kids (ages 2 and 4)

Medicine For Notes
Children's acetaminophen liquid (Tylenol) Fever, pain Check the concentration on the box matches your dosing chart
Children's ibuprofen liquid (Motrin, Advil) Fever, pain, swelling Give with food; don't use if vomiting or dehydrated
Children's allergy medicine labeled for age 2+ (cetirizine or loratadine liquid) Allergies, hives, itching Ask the pediatrician what to use for a sudden allergic reaction
Oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte or similar) Vomiting, diarrhea, heat Liquid bottles plus powder packets
Saline nose drops and a nasal aspirator Stuffy nose, colds Children's cough and cold medicines are not recommended under age 4
Honey Cough (over age 1) A spoonful before bed for the cough
Diaper rash cream (zinc oxide) Rash For the 2-year-old
Hydrocortisone 1% cream Bug bites, itchy rashes Small amounts, short use
Children's sunscreen and insect repellent (picaridin or DEET) Outdoor time Mosquitoes increase when water stands after storms

For the adults

Medicine For
Acetaminophen and ibuprofen (or naproxen) Pain, fever
Antihistamines: cetirizine or loratadine (non-drowsy), diphenhydramine Allergies, hives, sleep
Loperamide (Imodium) Diarrhea (adults only)
Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) Upset stomach (adults only; not for children)
Antacids and famotidine Heartburn
Meclizine Nausea, motion sickness on long drives
Electrolyte packets Heat, illness
Lubricating eye drops, lip balm Dry air, smoke

For everyone

  • Antibiotic ointment, hydrocortisone cream, burn gel, aloe
  • Oral rehydration solution and electrolyte packets
  • Each person's prescriptions: 2-week supply minimum, plus a written list of names, doses, prescribing doctor and pharmacy
  • Any prescribed epinephrine auto-injector or inhaler: keep a spare in the go-bag
  • Glasses or spare contacts and solution

Storing medicines safely

  • Lock everything in a box kept up high. In a crowded apartment during an outage, a 2-year-old finding pills is a bigger danger than most illnesses; poison control is 1-800-222-1222.
  • Keep medicines in the warm room in winter and out of a hot car in summer; heat ruins many liquids.
  • Check expiration dates every 6 months (set a reminder for when the clocks change) and replace what's expired.
  • Insulin and other refrigerated prescriptions go in a cooler with ice packs; check the package insert for how long they last at room temperature.
  • If someone in the house depends on powered medical equipment, register with the State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry (STEAR) by calling 211.

First-aid kit

  • ☐ Gauze pads and rolls, adhesive bandages in several sizes, medical tape
  • ☐ Elastic bandage, triangular bandage, trauma shears
  • ☐ Tourniquet (CAT or SOF-T style) and a pressure bandage
  • ☐ Digital thermometer (ear or forehead types are easiest with toddlers)
  • ☐ Children's and adult fever/pain relievers (acetaminophen, ibuprofen), with their measuring tools
  • ☐ Oral rehydration solution packets or Pedialyte
  • ☐ Antihistamine (for allergic reactions), hydrocortisone cream, antibiotic ointment
  • ☐ Tweezers, saline wound wash, nitrile gloves, hand sanitizer
  • ☐ Burn gel dressings, instant cold packs, hand warmers
  • ☐ Emergency (mylar) blankets
  • ☐ Copies of insurance cards and the medication list
Kids: ages 2 and 4

Toddlers lose heat and fluids faster than adults and can't always tell you they feel sick, so the kids set the household's limits: when the house becomes unsafe for the 2-year-old, it's time to go.

Food and drink

  • Two weeks of foods they already eat: shelf-stable milk boxes, fruit and applesauce pouches, crackers, dry cereal, peanut butter (if no allergy), granola bars, canned fruit.
  • Choking risk for the 2-year-old: no whole nuts, popcorn or hard candy; cut grapes and hot-dog pieces lengthwise.
  • Spill-proof cups filled with bottled or boiled water; offer a drink every hour, more in heat.
  • Hungry, tired toddlers melt down fast: keep snack times on their usual schedule.

Warm and safe at night

  • One more layer than an adult: thermal top and bottoms, fleece pajamas, wool socks, a hat.
  • Everyone sleeps together in the warm room. Blankets are fine at this age, but keep heavy piles away from the 2-year-old's face.
  • Check the back of the neck or chest, not hands: cold red skin, unusual fussiness, clumsiness or sleepiness means they need warming.
  • Keep both kids well away from any heat source, candle or camp stove; a toddler gate across a doorway helps.

Hot weather

  • Light clothes, shade, cool damp washcloths, a battery fan.
  • Offer water often; watch for peeing less than usual, the first sign of dehydration.
  • Never leave either child in a parked car, even for a minute.

Diapers, potty and hygiene

  • If the 2-year-old is in diapers or pull-ups: a 2-week supply (roughly 6 a day), wipes, rash cream, plastic bags.
  • A portable potty with disposable liners works when toilets can't flush and keeps a potty-trained 4-year-old on track.
  • Hand sanitizer before every snack; stomach bugs spread fast through a family with little water.

Keeping kids calm

  • Keep meals, naps and bedtime on the usual schedule as much as you can.
  • Give each child their own small flashlight or glow stick; no candles in reach.
  • An outage box with books, crayons, cards, stickers, play-dough, puzzles and a comfort toy for each.
  • Explain simply that the lights are off and the grown-ups have a plan. Kids take their cue from your tone.

Teach them now

  • The 4-year-old: full name, your full names, your phone number (a little song helps) and that our meeting point is home, our apartment (practice saying the building and unit number).
  • The 2-year-old: their name and yours. Write your phone number inside their jacket or on a wristband.
  • Both: find a firefighter or police officer if lost; never touch wires, generators, heaters or candles.
  • During any emergency, take a full-length phone photo of each child every morning. If one gets separated, you'll have what they're wearing today.
Other Austin hazards that cause outages

Central Texas is one of the most flash-flood-prone regions in the country, and storms that knock out power often bring flooding, tornadoes or extreme heat with them.

Hazard Warning What your family does
Flash flood Flash Flood Warning on phone, radio or NOAA radio Never drive or walk into moving water: about 6 inches can knock an adult down and 12 inches can float a car. Turn around, don't drown. Check ATXfloods.com for closed low-water crossings before driving. A second-floor unit is above most flooding, so staying put is usually safest.
Tornado Tornado Warning, outdoor sirens Go to the lowest floor you can reach quickly, in an interior hallway or room away from windows. From the second floor, a ground-floor interior stairwell or a neighbor's downstairs unit is better than staying up top; if you can't get down, use an interior bathroom or closet. Shoes on, helmets or pillows over the kids' heads.
Extreme heat Heat Advisory, Excessive Heat Warning Second-floor units get hottest. Follow the heat steps above; with no A/C, leave for a cooling center or Fallback 1 by early afternoon.
Wildfire Evacuation order, smoke Southwest Austin borders greenbelt. Leave immediately when told; keep go-bags by the door during red-flag fire weather. Close windows and run a portable air purifier if smoke is heavy.
Ice storm, freeze Winter Storm Warning Expect power and water outages lasting days (Feb 2021, Feb 2023). Fill water, charge everything and fuel the car before it arrives.
Safety, security and evacuation

Leave early, in daylight, with a full tank, rather than late on icy or dark roads. Decide each evening using the thresholds below.

Time to leave (rules of thumb)

Situation Leave when
Cold, with the 2- and 4-year-old The warm room can't stay above about 16°C
Cold, adults and older kids The warm room can't stay above about 13°C, or anyone shows hypothermia signs
Heat Indoors stays above about 32°C, or anyone shows heat-exhaustion signs
Water No running water and stored water will run out within 2 days
Medical Any medicine or device can't be kept going
Fire or official order Immediately; don't wait for power to return

Fallback locations

Agree on these now and fill in the blanks, so the decision to leave is quick: when a "Time to leave" line above is crossed, go to Fallback 1; if the outage is citywide or past 3 days, go to Fallback 2.

Tier What to look for Name, address, phone (fill in)
Fallback 1: nearby (15 to 30 min) Friends or family in another part of Austin, on a different power grid area, ideally in a house with gas heat or a generator
Fallback 2: out of town (1 to 3 hours) Family, friends or a hotel outside the outage: San Antonio, Waco, College Station or Houston, depending on where the outage is
Backup hotel A family room or suite booked by phone before you drive; hotels in the outage area fill fast or lose power too
Public option, daytime Warming or cooling center: Hampton Library at Oak Hill, 5125 Convict Hill Rd, during open hours, or as announced on KLBJ 590 AM 512-974-9900
Public option, overnight City cold-weather shelter; registration times and a ride via the hotline or 311 512-972-5055

How to leave

  1. Text your out-of-state contact where you're going and when you expect to arrive.
  2. Grab the go-bags (one per adult plus the kids' bag), the medicine kit, documents and chargers.
  3. Check both car seats are in the car; load water, snacks, blankets and the kids' comfort items.
  4. Pack still-cold fridge and freezer food in a cooler.
  5. In a freeze: shut off your unit's water valve and open the faucets to drain the lines.
  6. Unplug appliances, lock up, and tell the leasing office and a neighbor you've left (don't leave a note on the door saying the unit is empty).
  7. Drive in daylight, on a full tank, by the routes below.

Routes out (check the radio for closures)

  • North: Brodie Ln or MoPac (Loop 1) to US-290 / Ben White and central Austin.
  • West: US-290 west from Oak Hill toward Dripping Springs.
  • South and east: W Slaughter Ln east to I-35, then south to San Marcos or north through town.
  • Southwest Austin borders wooded greenbelt: in a wildfire, follow official evacuation orders, leave immediately, and don't wait to pack.

Go-bag (one per adult, plus a kid bag)

  • ☐ 3 days of water and no-cook food, plus kids' snacks and milk boxes
  • ☐ Diapers, wipes, change of clothes per person, warm layers, rain gear
  • ☐ Medications, medication list, first-aid kit, glasses
  • ☐ Phone chargers, power bank, small battery radio, headlamp, spare batteries
  • ☐ Cash in small bills (card readers and ATMs fail without power)
  • ☐ Copies of IDs, insurance cards, birth certificates, a printed copy of this plan
  • ☐ Comfort item and a small activity for each child
  • ☐ Pet food, leash and carrier, if you have pets

Safety at home and on the road

  • Downed power line: stay at least 35 ft away, assume it's live, call 911 and Austin Energy.
  • Dark traffic signal: treat the intersection as an all-way stop.
  • Flashlights and headlamps, not candles. If you must use candles, an adult stays in the room and they sit in a sturdy holder away from kids, curtains and bedding.
  • Smoke alarms and CO alarms with fresh batteries in every sleeping area.
  • Lock doors and keep a light visible at night; dark neighborhoods see more break-ins.
  • Scams spike after disasters: Austin Energy will never demand payment by phone to restore service.
  • When power returns: plug appliances back one at a time over several minutes; check food temperatures before eating.
  • Apartment fire or smoke: leave by the stairs immediately with the kids, close your door behind you, never use an elevator. Keep a headlamp and shoes by the front door.
  • Burst pipe or leak: shut your unit's water valve (find it now) and call emergency maintenance; water through the floor reaches the unit below fast.
Supplies and prep this week

The tasks below take one weekend and cover most of what makes an outage dangerous. Supplies are sized per person for 14 days; for your household of 4, multiply by four (56 gallons of water, about 110 to 170 meals).

Do this week

  • ☐ Print this document (export to PDF) and put copies in the kitchen and each car.
  • ☐ Download offline maps: in Google Maps, search 78749, tap your profile, Offline maps, Select your own map, and cover southwest Austin to downtown.
  • ☐ Register at WarnCentralTexas.org for alerts at your home address; text REG to 287846 for Austin Energy outage alerts.
  • ☐ Buy a battery carbon monoxide alarm for the sleeping room and test all smoke alarms.
  • ☐ Buy a battery or hand-crank AM/FM/NOAA weather radio and tune it to KLBJ 590 AM.
  • ☐ Find your main water shutoff and breaker panel; label the breaker for the water heater.
  • ☐ Fill in the family communication table and put contact cards in wallets and backpacks.
  • ☐ Keep the car's tank at least half full and $200 or more in small bills at home.
  • ☐ Check your lease and renter's insurance: what's covered if food spoils or a pipe bursts, and the after-hours maintenance number.
  • ☐ Walk both stairways out of your building at night with a headlamp, carrying the 2-year-old.

Supply checklist (per person, 14 days)

Category Amount Notes
Drinking water 14 gallons Plus extra for kids' cups and pets
No-cook food 28 to 42 meals Canned protein, beans, peanut butter, crackers, cereal, dried fruit, nuts
Kids' food and milk boxes 2 weeks Foods they already eat, spill-proof cups
Diapers or pull-ups and wipes (2-year-old) 2 weeks Roughly 6 a day
Prescriptions 2 weeks minimum Plus a written medication list
Warm layers 1 set Thermal base layer, fleece, hat, gloves, wool socks
Sleeping warmth 1 sleeping bag or 2 heavy blankets Plus fleece pajamas and a hat for each child
Light 1 headlamp Plus 2 lanterns for the household and spare batteries
Power 1 power bank per adult Plus a power station and solar panel for longer outages
Hygiene 1 kit Toilet paper, hand sanitizer, wet wipes, heavy trash bags, bleach (unscented)
Cooking Household Propane camp stove (outdoor use), 2 spare cylinders, manual can opener, matches
Cash Household Small bills

Nice to have

  • Battery or solar fans for summer outages
  • Two-way radios (FRS/GMRS) for talking to neighbors when cell service is down
  • 5-gallon bucket with lid and kitty litter for sanitation
  • Collapsible water containers and a gravity water filter
  • Fire extinguisher (ABC rated) in the kitchen

Keeping the kit ready

A kit only works if it's current. Tie these checks to dates you already remember.

When Check
Every month Power banks and power station charged; flashlights work; car tank at least half full
Spring and fall (when the clocks change) Smoke and CO alarm batteries; medicine expiration dates; swap kids' spare clothes for their current size; rotate stored water you filled yourself
Every fall, before freeze season Re-check phone numbers and fallback contacts; refresh the 3-day menu with foods the kids eat now; practice the stairway walk at night
Every spring, before storm and heat season Fans and cooling items ready; update the go-bags; review flood and tornado steps with the kids
After every use Replace what you used within a week

As-of this plan: phone numbers and locations checked October 2026. Re-check each fall before winter.
